- **Verbal destruction:** the obsessional's fear that words or thoughts harm the Other reveals that the destructive act is already structured by signifiers.
- **Blasphemy:** a privileged signifier is lowered to the status of an object; the operation is useful as a model for obsessional verbal degradation.

### Examples, cases, texts, and wordplay

Lacan recommends Glover's "The Therapeutic Effect of Inexact Interpretation" because it shows that the practitioner can reinforce symptom structure through a theoretically misguided intervention even when the intervention is apparently therapeutic.

Winnicott's transitional object is invoked to argue against a theory that makes frustration the sole motor of symbolic development. The small object appears in the zone opened when satisfaction no longer exhausts the child's relation to the mother.

The Rat Man supplies the most vivid example of verbal destruction. In childhood rage he insults his father with nouns such as "towel" and "plate". Lacan reads this not as random childish abuse but as a reduction of the paternal Other to interchangeable objects.

The Casimir-Perier anecdote at the end satirizes the imaginary satisfaction of demand. A man asks for freedom; Casimir-Perier responds, in effect, "You have it", and escapes, leaving the demand formally satisfied but structurally untouched. Lacan uses the joke to characterize an analytic solution that grants the requested object without interpreting the desire carried by the demand.

### Schemas, formulas, and notation

[FIGURE: The hysteric's circuit]

Source location: Chapter XXVI, around printed p. 444.

Description: Lacan contrasts two parallel supports of hysterical desire. One lies on the level of idealization and symbolic identification, the other on the imaginary level through `i(a)`, the image of the little other. The circuit shows how the hysteric can use an identification to another person as a relay for posing the question of desire in the Other.

[FIGURE: The obsessional's circuit]

Source location: Chapter XXVI, around printed p. 445.

Description: the circuit is organized around the obsessional's relation to demand and culminates in the destructive formulation "who kills me". The graph is intended to show that the obsessional attacks the Other through signifiers while at the same time preserving the Other through the very act of articulation.

Relevant notation includes:

- `$ ◊ D` for the divided subject in relation to demand
- `d` for desire
- `i(a)` for the image of the little other
- the phallus as privileged signifier of desire
- `S(Ⱥ)` in the background as the signifier of the barred Other

### Relation to the seminar's developing argument

Chapter XXVI extends the previous chapter's critique of suggestive treatment into a more general theory of interpretation and then differentiates the circuits of hysterical and obsessional desire. The movement is important because Lacan no longer treats the graph only as a map of demand and desire. He uses it to distinguish structures. The obsessional is not defined by a stock of aggressive or anal contents but by a characteristic signifying relation in which the Other's desire is negated and preserved at once. This sets up the next session's attempt to explain regression, symptom, psychosis, and neurosis from the same structural coordinates.

### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, Book V: Formations of the Unconscious*, ed. Jacques-Alain Miller, trans. Russell Grigg, Polity, 2017, Chapter XXVI, printed pp. 432-447.


## Chapter XXVII. Exiting via the Symptom

**Primary source:** Polity 2017, printed pp. 448-464  
**Session date:** 25 June 1958

### Argument and progression

Lacan continues the critique of the female obsessional case but begins by clarifying what kind of object a neurosis is. A neurosis is not a foreign thing attached to an otherwise intact personality. Nor is it exhausted by a collection of discrete symptoms that can be removed one by one. The structure is present in the subject's conduct, relations, recurrent choices, ways of speaking, and ways of moving between the little other and the big Other. In this sense the subject's whole pattern of behaviour can be read as a kind of speech.

Lacan makes the claim as strongly as possible: hysterical or obsessional conduct is **structured like a language**. This does not mean that every gesture has a dictionary meaning. It means that the subject's history is articulated as a signifying sequence whose sense is not consciously available to the subject. The neurotic's behaviour can therefore be called a form of "full speech" while remaining cryptographic. The barred subject speaks through symptoms, acts, silences, repetitions, and relational patterns without knowing the message being articulated.

This brings Lacan back to the status of the Other. The Other is first the locus of speech, instituted whenever the subject speaks. But the upper line of the graph indicates a further dimension that Lacan calls, in this session, the **Other of the Other**: the place in which the Other's own speech takes shape. The paradox of the unconscious follows from this. The subject addresses an Other through demand but does not know what his demand is for that Other, because the Other is not merely a neutral code. The Other is itself implicated as a desiring being. The opacity of the Other's desire is what makes the response to demand opaque to the subject.

This is the structural sense of the formula that **the unconscious is the discourse of the Other**. The phrase does not mean that an external person secretly controls the subject. It means that the signifying articulation that determines the subject is produced in the field opened by speech and by the Other's response, and that the subject encounters it as something spoken in him from elsewhere. The unconscious is articulated but not immediately articulable by the conscious ego.

Lacan then recasts **regression**. Regression is not an actual return of the adult to an infantile organism. The analysand does not biologically become oral, anal, or infantile again. What returns are signifiers. An "oral phase" or an "anal phase" names the persistence and renewed use of signifiers that were organized at particular moments of the subject's history. A fixation is the continuing predominance of one such signifying system. Regression occurs when analysis reopens the history of demand and these earlier signifiers are taken up again in the subject's present discourse.

This is why Lacan says that **regression is regression of discourse**. The analytic setting does not reproduce childhood literally. By inviting speech and by refusing to satisfy demand at face value, it reopens the signifying forms through which demand was historically articulated. Oral, anal, and other images matter because they have become detached from immediate biological need and acquired a signifying function. An adult oral fixation is not explained by a persisting need for food; an anal fixation does not mean an adult need for excrement. The bodily image has been isolated, mortified, and made to function as a signifier.

The same point revises the concept of **drive**. Lacan notes the problem of translating Freud's *Trieb* and rejects the idea that the analytic drive is simply animal instinct. Analytic experience concerns the subject's dependence on signifiers that borrow their material from bodily zones and organs. The drive is therefore meaningful to analysis because bodily functions have been caught in a signifying economy. This is what differentiates the human subject from the animal model that repeatedly tempts psychology.

Lacan then returns to the paternal metaphor. The mother's desire initially appears opaque. The Name-of-the-Father intervenes as the signifier that metaphorizes this desire and produces the phallus as a signified. The paternal metaphor does not supply information about the empirical father. It gives the subject a symbolic means of locating the desire of the Other. This is the structural operation that makes the Other's desire legible enough to be inserted into an unconscious articulation.

The contrast with psychosis clarifies the argument. When the Name-of-the-Father is foreclosed, the metaphorical effect is not produced in the same way and the mother's desire is not symbolized through the paternal signifier. Lacan does not say that the psychotic subject encounters no Other. On the contrary, the Other can become overwhelmingly present. What would have been unconscious speech can instead return as speech that addresses the subject from the field of perception. The world speaks. Lacan uses the familiar example of a red car acquiring a direct, personal signification for a delusional subject. The failure is not absence of signification but the failure of the signifying mediation that would ordinarily locate it within the paternal metaphor.

This lets Lacan distinguish **psychotic negation** from the obsessional's operation. The obsessional has not failed to symbolize the Other's desire in the same way. His structure retains the full constellation of the symbolic coordinates. What he does is negate or undo the Other's desire after it has been symbolized. Lacan invokes *Verneinung*: the signifier is admitted and at the same time marked with a "No". This is quite different from foreclosure. The obsessional's elaborate undoing presupposes the symbolic field he is attempting to neutralize.

Undoing is therefore a signifying operation. One cannot undo what has never entered articulation. The obsessional places a signifier in parentheses, cancels it, repeats it, separates it from another, or constructs a counter-formula. Isolation and defence work in the same register. These operations become necessary because the obsessional's demand contains a destructive dimension. Lacan increasingly names it a **demand for death**. The demand threatens the Other, but because the Other is also the condition for the subject's own symbolic existence, the obsessional must preserve what he attacks.

This is the contradiction at the centre of obsession. The subject must maintain the Other while simultaneously undoing the Other's desire. His rituals, thoughts, doubts, cancellations, and defensive separations are all attempts to regulate this impossible task. The phallus is centrally implicated because it marks the place of the Other's desire. To undo the phallus as signifier is to attack the point at which the Other's desire would be acknowledged.

Lacan then states the direction of analytic work in a formula that anticipates the next year's seminar. The subject has to assume genital desire not merely as an organism but as a speaking subject. This means making the phallus function as a signifier of desire. The "phallic stage" should therefore not be understood as a biological stage distinct from a later genital maturity. Its analytic importance lies in the signifying structuration of genital desire.

At the upper level of the graph, the desired outcome is homologous to what "full speech" accomplishes on the lower level. The subject must reach a point at which he can locate himself in the signifying articulation of desire. Lacan explicitly rejects the formula "I am the phallus". The movement is instead toward recognizing the place the phallus occupies in the structure and recognizing oneself as a subject who is **not** identical with that signifier. This is how Lacan reads Freud's `Wo Es war, soll Ich werden`: the subject is to come to the place where the signifying determination operated, not to inflate the ego into mastery.

From this point Lacan contrasts the characteristic detours of hysteria and obsession. The hysteric takes an imaginary detour through an identification with another person in order to locate the question of desire. Dora's identification with Herr K. is again the model: the image of the little other provides a position from which the enigma of the woman's desirability can be posed.

The obsessional also uses the image of the other, but differently. He constructs what Lacan calls a fortress or stronghold of the ego. A friend, brother, rival, or admired man can function as an image of virility, strength, precedence, or phallic power. The obsessional supplements himself with this image while keeping his own desire at a protected distance. Here the phallus appears not primarily as symbolic signifier but as imaginary prestige.

This distinction is decisive in Lacan's criticism of the treatment. The analyst has increasingly occupied the place of the little other for the patient, a benevolent and powerful man who authorizes her to possess the phallus. The initial difficulty in speaking was tied to the big Other and to the destructive demand; later, the patient simply does not want to speak because the analyst has been installed as an imaginary figure within the very economy that should have been interpreted. The treatment therefore shifts from interpretation toward suggestion.

Lacan's description is deliberately stark. The analyst, as benevolent maternal figure and masculine model, effectively tells the patient that she may absorb the phallus, trust him, become stronger, and abandon guilt. The patient's fantasies are not traversed as signifying formations; they are ratified as routes to an identification. The obsessions persist, but their guilt is reduced. The treatment ends in a euphoric or quasi-manic state of power and goodness.

The patient's decision to send her eldest son to the analyst becomes, in this context, an **acting out** of what the analysis has missed. The child occupies a symbolic place that the treatment failed to elucidate. The patient hands the phallic problem back to the analyst through the son. Lacan takes this as evidence that the final state is not a resolution of the neurosis but a successful transformation of one of its mechanisms into a more acceptable symptom.

The chapter's title, "Exiting via the Symptom", is therefore pointed. An analysis can produce an exit that is really a rearrangement of the symptom. A patient may feel better and become less guilty while the central signifying structure remains untouched. Lacan is not denying therapeutic change. He is asking whether symptom relief produced by an imaginary identification should be confused with the analytic elucidation of desire.

### Concepts and distinctions

- **Neurosis as structure:** the neurosis is expressed throughout conduct and relational style, not merely in isolated symptoms.
- **Cryptographic full speech:** the subject articulates a structured history through behaviour and symptoms without consciously knowing its sense.
- **Unconscious as discourse of the Other:** the unconscious is the signifying articulation produced in the field of the Other and encountered by the subject as speech from elsewhere.
- **Regression of discourse:** regression is the return of earlier signifiers of demand, not biological reversal to childhood.
- **Fixation:** persistence of a particular signifying organization, often using oral, anal, or other bodily images.
- **Drive / *Trieb*:** analytic drive concerns the subject's dependence on bodily signifiers, not a simple animal instinct.
- **Paternal metaphor:** the Name-of-the-Father symbolizes the mother's desire and produces the phallus as the relevant signification.
- **Foreclosure versus Verneinung:** psychosis involves foreclosure of the paternal signifier; obsession involves a negating or undoing operation within a symbolic field that remains constituted.
- **Phallus at symbolic and imaginary levels:** symbolically it marks the Other's desire; imaginarily it may appear as power, virility, prestige, or the image of a stronger semblable.
- **Acting out:** the patient's sending her son to the analyst is read as a showing of what has not been symbolically worked through.
- **Symptomatic exit:** therapeutic improvement can result from a more successful organization of the symptom without resolution of the underlying signifying question.

### Examples, cases, texts, and wordplay

Lacan uses the animal comparison negatively. The oral or anal images encountered in analysis are not evidence that humans simply retain animal instincts. Their clinical efficacy depends on their conversion into signifiers. This is part of the chapter's answer to what separates human drive from animal instinct.

Psychosis is illustrated through the way the field of perception can speak directly to the subject. A red car can become a message about immortality, not because the object intrinsically signifies immortality, but because the symbolic mediation that ordinarily limits and organizes the Other's address is compromised.

The female obsessional case again serves as the clinical test. Her progression from inability to speak to refusal to speak, the installation of the analyst as benevolent masculine image, persistent obsessions without guilt, and the final sending of her son to analysis are all used to distinguish interpretation from suggestion.

### Schemas, formulas, and notation

[FIGURE: Signifying chain and retroaction]

Source location: Chapter XXVII, around printed pp. 452-453.

Description: Lacan writes a sequence such as `S1 - S2 - S3 - S4` on an upper signifying line and places signification beneath it. Meaning is produced retroactively: later signifiers reshape the signification of earlier ones. This is the structural basis for treating fixation and regression as functions of discourse rather than literal chronological return.

[FIGURE: Paternal metaphor]

Source location: around printed p. 455.

Description: a metaphorical substitution places the Name-of-the-Father over the Mother's Desire and produces the phallus as signification. Lacan uses the schema to contrast neurotic symbolic organization with psychosis, where the paternal signifier is foreclosed and the metaphorical effect fails.

[FIGURE: Upper-level completion of the graph]

Source location: later part of Chapter XXVII.

Description: Lacan places the subject's confrontation with demand, the articulation of desire, the phallic signifier, and the Other on the upper level. The ideal analytic movement is toward a position in which the subject can locate himself where the phallus functions without identifying his being with it.

### Relation to the seminar's developing argument

Chapter XXVII consolidates the seminar's structural method just before the conclusion. Regression, drive, symptom, psychosis, hysteria, and obsession are all redescribed through the signifier. The chapter also explicitly points forward: the question of how interpretation gives access to the final articulation of desire will be the problem of the following year's seminar, *Desire and Its Interpretation*. Seminar V therefore closes not by completing a doctrine of desire but by establishing the coordinates from which desire can be interpreted.

### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, Book V: Formations of the Unconscious*, ed. Jacques-Alain Miller, trans. Russell Grigg, Polity, 2017, Chapter XXVII, printed pp. 448-464.


## Chapter XXVIII. You Are the One You Hate

**Primary source:** Polity 2017, printed pp. 465-481  
**Session date:** 2 July 1958

### Argument and progression

Lacan closes Seminar V by restating the wager of the entire year. The mechanisms discovered by Freud cannot be adequately described as tensions moving through a maturational sequence from pregenital to genital organization, nor can analytic experience be reduced to a theatre of identifications with mother, father, and other characters. Desire and its fixations become intelligible only when they are placed within the relations imposed by signifiers on the speaking subject. The graph of desire has been constructed as a way of locating these relations.

The final session takes the phallus as a test of whether this structural orientation has been understood. The phallus is "pluripresent" because it functions at several different places in the subject's economy. It may appear in symptom, fantasy, image, identification, rivalry, dream, or transferential relation, but its function is not identical in each place. A central error in interpretation is to assume that because the same phallic image recurs, it always means the same thing. Lacan's final critique of the female obsessional case is aimed precisely at this flattening.

He starts from the patient's pronounced **sense of guilt**. Obsessional thoughts are often experienced by the patient as intrusive and foreign, which creates a paradox: why should the subject feel guilty for thoughts that she simultaneously experiences as imposed upon her? Invoking the superego does not solve the problem unless the different levels involved are distinguished.

Lacan separates the **relationship to law** from the **sense of guilt**. Classical and religious accounts readily connect guilt to a violated law. Psychoanalysis reveals something more disquieting: guilt can arise without a consciously recognized law and may even intensify where the law's authority is weak. Lacan recalls the Pauline formula that the law makes sin, then reverses the familiar Dostoevskian proposition "if God does not exist, everything is permitted" into the analytic paradox that if God is dead, nothing is permitted. The point is not theological doctrine but the clinical fact that guilt is not simply proportional to an external prohibition.

Freud's discovery of Oedipal guilt is then relocated on the graph. Desire for the mother, paternal prohibition, and castration fantasy belong to different levels of the structure. The phallus can function as the signifier of the prohibition that strikes desire. The command that stands on the horizon of speech cannot simply be identified with the ordinary law or with a parental instruction. Lacan uses the Ten Commandments as an image for the structural laws of speech, and the command "Thou shalt not kill" becomes especially important because of the obsessional **demand for death**.

The Rat Man provides a model of the autonomous command. His obsessional imperatives appear as commands such as taking an examination or, at the extreme, cutting his own throat or killing an old woman. Psychosis makes the autonomy of command even more visible because commands may be directly heard and obeyed. In obsession, by contrast, the command is fragmented, veiled, and entangled in defensive procedures. The phenomenon nonetheless shows that command cannot be reduced to a consciously endorsed moral rule.

Lacan locates guilt more precisely in the relation between **demand and desire**. Guilt appears when a demand is experienced as forbidden because its formulation kills or extinguishes desire. It is therefore not identical with diffuse anxiety. The subject moves toward articulating a demand and finds that the movement threatens the very place from which desire could subsist. Because the subject cannot occupy every point of the graph at once, the structural relation appears phenomenologically as guilt.

This clarifies the obsessional's predicament. The obsessional's desire has been described as annulled but preserved, articulated in a form of *Verneinung*. He must defend the place of desire while his demands repeatedly threaten to extinguish it. The guilt surrounding aggressive, sacrilegious, or sexual thoughts belongs to this structure. It is not enough to tell the subject that the thoughts are harmless or to trace them to an instinctual quantity of aggressiveness. One has to determine how the demand is articulated and what happens to desire when it is articulated.

Lacan then distinguishes this upper-level command and guilt from what analytic theory calls the **archaic or maternal superego**. The latter belongs to the subject's earliest dependence on the first Other, the one who receives demands and gives or withholds satisfaction. The two levels can be confused because both involve prohibition and the Other, but they are not the same. The maternal superego belongs to the first economy of demand; the command and guilt that Lacan is analyzing arise on the upper horizon where desire and the Other of the Other are implicated.

This brings the chapter back to the demand for death. The demand for death is not simply a murderous instinct directed at a person. Because it is articulated as demand, it is already addressed to the Other. Its paradox is that the destruction of the Other would also destroy the very place in which demand can be made. Hence Lacan's formula that the **demand for death tends toward the death of demand**. The obsessional must therefore repeat, fragment, undo, and isolate his own formulations so that the Other is attacked without finally disappearing.

The case history makes this transgenerationally visible. The patient's mother is described as energetic, authoritative, and dominating, while the father, a corporal in the Gendarmerie, is gentle, unhappy, taciturn, jealous, and repeatedly defeated in the marital relation. The mother's attachment to an earlier, platonic love remains a persistent element in the parental field. Lacan resists the easy label of a "castrating mother" because it risks turning a structural relation into a personality judgment. What matters is that the demand for death appears to circulate in the parental couple without the mediation that would place the father securely as bearer of law.

The father's depression is reread accordingly. Rather than simply saying that the mother castrates him, Lacan links his misery to deprivation of a loved object and to a death wish turned back against himself. The parental drama gives the daughter an early encounter with a demand for death whose mediation is unstable. In the daughter's own neurosis, by contrast, the Oedipal horizon provides enough symbolic mediation for obsession rather than psychosis to form.

The phallus then reappears in several distinct **avatars**. One of the patient's earliest obsessions is fear of syphilitic contamination and of contaminating her eldest son. In this configuration she is not merely a woman envious of a male organ. Through the son she effectively occupies the position of one who "has" the phallus and fears its dangerous power. This alone shows why a single formula of penis envy cannot account for every phallic appearance.

Her obsessions of infanticide, poisoning, and harm are similarly linked to the demand for death. The phallus can appear here as the signifier of dangerous desire. Another obsession, fear that she may place pins in her parents' bed and prick her mother, gives the phallic signifier yet another form. The pin does not simply symbolize a penis in an invariant code. It appears at the point where desire, guilt, harm, and the maternal relation intersect.

Religious obsessions provide another register. Lacan notes that Christianity gives obsessional symptomatology a particularly rich symbolic mould because of its doctrines of Word, incarnation, sacrifice, commandment, and guilt. The Christian Logos, the Word made flesh, is relevant because Seminar V has repeatedly asked how the signifier marks the living body. The patient's fantasy of crushing the head of Christ, whose face resembles the analyst's, is therefore not adequately read as simple penis envy or aggression toward a male possessor. At that stage of transference the analyst stands for the effects of the signifier and the patient's relation to speech.

A later dream in which the patient sees a breast replaced by a phallus, or a phallus situated between the breasts, again shows the danger of treating phallic imagery as a single message. The image can become "polyphallic" and approach the form of the many-breasted Diana of Ephesus. The visual multiplication itself warns against reducing the image to a one-to-one organ symbol. The question is what structural position the phallus occupies at that moment.

The shoe material provides another shift of function. After the analyst has established an equivalence between shoes and phallus, the patient dreams of having her shoe repaired and then standing on a balcony decorated with blue, white, and red paper lanterns, surrounded by men while her mother admires her from below. Lacan reads the scene less as a confession of masculine identification than as an exhibition before the maternal third party. The phallus is functioning in the image of the body and the semblable as a sign of power, prestige, and desirability.

The lesson is methodological: the same signifier can appear in different places of the graph and therefore serve different functions. A symptom, a fantasy, an imaginary identification, and a signifier of the barred Other are not interchangeable merely because each includes a phallic image. Interpretation must first locate the level at which the element is functioning.

Lacan then evaluates the therapeutic outcome. The analyst has largely authorized the patient's phallic fantasies and recoded them as legitimate possession. In doing so he has reduced her guilt, but her obsessions remain. Lacan compares this to teaching her to love her obsessions. The treatment ends with euphoric, narcissistic feelings of strength and goodness, yet the author himself recognizes the incompleteness of the result. Lacan links the outcome directly to the mode of interpretation: the treatment has reduced and accommodated demand rather than elucidating the demand for death and its relation to desire.

This is why he proposes replacing the vague language of "aggressiveness" with the more structurally precise **demand for death** where appropriate. The phrase locates aggression within speech and demand. It asks who is being addressed, what place the Other occupies, and what happens to desire through the articulation of destruction.

The seminar concludes with the Christian commandment **"Love your neighbour as yourself."** Lacan treats it not as a moral platitude but as a linguistic problem. The phrase cannot simply mean that the ego should be the model of benevolence, since analytic experience shows that the subject's relation to himself is anything but harmonious. Nor is the first-person paraphrase "I love my neighbour as myself" adequate. The force of the commandment lies in the second-person address.

Placed in the locus of the Other, the commandment forms a circuit parallel to the obsessional formulation "You are the one who kills me." The "yourself" is not simply the ego but the `tu`, the thou, encountered in speech. The neighbour can therefore be recognized as the one hated in the demand for death precisely because the subject does not know this hatred as his own. The title, `Tu es celui que tu hais`, "You are the one you hate", is homophonic in French with `Tu es celui que tu es`, "You are the one you are". The wordplay condenses the chapter's argument: subjective identity is reached not by egoic self-recognition but through the return of one's own signifying position from the Other.

Lacan links this final formulation to Freud's `Wo Es war, soll Ich werden` and to the wisdom formula "You are that." The analytic task is for the subject to assume where he is on the horizon of his own speech. The conclusion therefore returns to the year's opening thesis. Formations of the unconscious are not detachable contents hidden beneath consciousness. They are the signifying forms through which the subject is constituted, divided, and addressed.

### Concepts and distinctions

- **Law versus guilt:** guilt is not merely the subjective effect of violating an explicit law. It can arise structurally in the relation between demand and desire.
- **Command:** the command occupies the upper horizon of speech and can manifest autonomously, especially clearly in obsession and psychosis.
- **Demand for death:** an articulated demand that aims at the Other's destruction while depending on the Other as the locus of demand.
- **Death of demand:** if the Other were actually destroyed, the place from which demand can be addressed would disappear. This gives obsessional destruction its circular form.
- **Maternal/archaic superego:** linked to early dependence on the first Other and the economy of demand; distinct from the upper-level relation of command, guilt, and desire.
- **Guilt and desire:** guilt appears where the formulation of a prohibited demand extinguishes or threatens desire.
- **Phallus as pluripresent signifier:** the phallus can function differently in symptom, fantasy, dream, transference, imaginary identification, and the signifier of the barred Other.
- **Penis envy:** clinically real as material but inadequate as a universal explanation for the different phallic positions found in the case.
- **Interpretive localization:** an element's meaning depends on where and how it functions in the structure, not on a fixed symbolic dictionary.
- **`Wo Es war, soll Ich werden`:** interpreted as the subject's assumption of the place in which unconscious signification has operated, rather than as ego mastery.

### Examples, cases, texts, and wordplay

The Rat Man's command phenomena illustrate the autonomous imperative. The subject can imagine commands to take an examination, cut his own throat, or kill an old woman, showing that the command cannot be explained simply by conscious intention.

The patient's parental history is central. Her mother dominates the family field; her father, a gendarme, is gentle, depressed, jealous, and repeatedly defeated. Lacan uses the configuration to distinguish a structural demand for death from the simplifying label "castrating mother".

The patient's symptoms and dreams supply several different phallic functions:

- fear of syphilitic contamination and of contaminating her son;
- obsessions of infanticide and poisoning;
- fear of putting pins in the parents' bed and pricking the mother;
- the fantasy of crushing Christ's head, with the head resembling the analyst;
- the dream of a phallus replacing a breast or located between the breasts;
- the shoe-repair and balcony dream, with the mother admiring her among men.

The translator's endnote clarifies the title's wordplay: `Tu es celui que tu hais` ("You are the one you hate") and `Tu es celui que tu es` ("You are the one you are") are homophonic. The pun is conceptually important because the final session ties hatred, address, identification, and subjective assumption to the second-person `tu`.

### Schemas, formulas, and notation

[FIGURE: Three levels of command, desire, and demand]

Source location: Chapter XXVIII, especially the discussion of guilt and superego around printed pp. 470-473.

Description: Lacan superimposes three levels corresponding to the upper horizon of command, the middle level of desire, and the lower level of demand. The point is to prevent the archaic maternal superego, the commandment, and guilt from being collapsed into one agency. Guilt emerges in the relation between demand and desire, while the command occupies the upper horizon.

[FIGURE: Recurrent locations of the phallus signifier]

Source location: throughout the second half of Chapter XXVIII.

Description: no single new diagram is introduced, but Lacan uses the established graph to distinguish several appearances of the phallus: as signifier of dangerous desire in the symptom, as image of power in the relation to the semblable, as transferential signifier, and at `S(Ⱥ)` as linked to the barred Other. The same phallic content must therefore be localized structurally before it is interpreted.

### Relation to the seminar's developing argument

The final chapter functions as both case critique and retrospective synthesis. It returns to the central thesis that the unconscious is structured through signifiers, demonstrates why apparently identical phallic images cannot be interpreted uniformly, and places guilt and aggression inside the dialectic of demand and desire. The concluding commandment and the phrase "You are the one you hate" bring the seminar back to address, the Other, and full speech. Seminar V thus ends by opening the question of how the subject can assume the desire articulated in the Other, which is the explicit bridge to Seminar VI.

### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, Book V: Formations of the Unconscious*, ed. Jacques-Alain Miller, trans. Russell Grigg, Polity, 2017, Chapter XXVIII, printed pp. 465-481.
- Russell Grigg, translator's endnote to the title of Chapter XXVIII, clarifying the homophony between `Tu es celui que tu hais` and `Tu es celui que tu es`.


## Appendix A. The Graph of Desire

**Primary source:** Polity 2017, printed p. 485  
**Status:** Editorial appendix reproducing the later complete form of the graph for orientation

### Source status and caution

The appendix is essential for navigation but must not be mistaken for a diagram that appeared in this complete form during every session of Seminar V. The editorial note states that the schema elaborated across the seminar later acquired its definitive form in Lacan's 1962 text "The Subversion of the Subject and the Dialectic of Desire in the Freudian Unconscious". The appendix reproduces that complete graph and notes that it was preceded by several stages of development.

For this corpus file, the complete graph is therefore used as a **retrospective map of coordinates developed during Seminar V**, not as evidence that every label and every relation was already fixed in November 1957. The session-by-session reconstruction above preserves the progressive construction of the schema and should control any question about when a particular relation first became explicit.

### Descriptive reconstruction of the complete graph

[FIGURE: Complete Graph of Desire]

Source location: Appendix A, printed p. 485. The rendered primary page was inspected directly because the visual structure is not adequately preserved by text extraction.

The graph is composed of two vertically stacked signifying circuits, crossed by a roughly vertical trajectory linking the subject at the bottom to the upper field of desire.

At the **lower level**:

- the left circular node is `s(A)`, the signification/message produced in relation to the Other;
- the right circular node is `A`, the Other as locus of the signifier and speech;
- the lower-left terminal is `I(A)`, the ego ideal / ideal point associated with the Other;
- the lower-right terminal is the barred subject, conventionally written `$`;
- `m` appears on the left lower vertical side;
- `i(a)` appears on the right lower side, marking the imaginary image of the little other;
- an inner horizontal arrow runs from the right toward the left, while a curved upper arc links the two lower nodes in the opposite direction;
- the side labels "Signifier" and "Voice" indicate two effects associated with the lower signifying circuit.

This lower level condenses material developed throughout the seminar concerning code and message, demand, the Other, retroaction, the ego, the image of the other, and identification. Need is not represented as a pure biological line. The subject enters the graph already caught in signifying and imaginary relations.

At the **upper level**:

- the left circular node is `S(Ⱥ)`, the signifier of the barred Other;
- the right circular node is `($ ◊ D)`, the divided subject in relation to demand;
- the left side carries `($ ◊ a)`, the fantasy relation, adjacent to the label "Jouissance";
- `d` appears on the right side, indicating desire;
- "Castration" is marked to the right of the upper circuit;
- as below, the inner horizontal arrow runs back across the circuit while curved arcs indicate the return and retroaction of signification.

The upper level formalizes the seminar's central distinction between **demand and desire**. The subject's demand is articulated in the Other, but desire emerges in the interval opened by the impossibility of demand exhausting what is at stake. `S(Ⱥ)` marks that the Other itself lacks a final signifier that could close the system. The fantasy relation `$ ◊ a` provides a support for desire in relation to this lack. Castration marks the symbolic operation through which the phallus comes to function as the privileged signifier of desire.

The two levels must be read together. The lower level is not merely conscious and the upper level merely unconscious in a simple spatial sense. Rather, the graph distinguishes different circuits of signification. The lower circuit concerns articulated demand and the return of a message; the upper circuit concerns what is produced by the signifier beyond the satisfiable content of demand. The seminar's analyses of wit, paternal metaphor, Oedipus, phallus, hysteria, obsession, transference, symptom, and guilt can be placed on these circuits without being reduced to one another.

### Major relations consolidated by the graph

1. **Retroaction:** meaning is produced after the fact. A later signifier can alter the signification of what preceded it. This structure was already introduced in the early chapters through the sentence and the witticism.
2. **Other and message:** the subject's speech crosses the locus of the Other and returns as a message that can have a different sense from conscious intention.
3. **Demand:** need becomes human demand only by being articulated in signifiers and addressed to the Other.
4. **Desire:** desire is not another need but the remainder or interval produced by the articulation of demand, especially where demand for love exceeds any satisfiable request.
5. **Barred Other:** the Other cannot supply the final signifier of the subject's being. `S(Ⱥ)` gives formal expression to this structural non-completion.
6. **Fantasy:** `$ ◊ a` gives desire a support in the relation between the divided subject and the object-position represented by `a`. In this file the notation is retained without importing the fully elaborated later theory of object `a` back into Seminar V.
7. **Castration and phallus:** castration is a symbolic operation and the phallus functions as the privileged signifier of desire, not merely as an anatomical organ.
8. **Imaginary support:** `m` and `i(a)` preserve the mirror-stage dimension inside the graph. Desire is symbolic but repeatedly takes support from identifications with the little other.
9. **Ideal identification:** `I(A)` marks the relation to the ideal point in the Other and helps distinguish ego ideal from the imaginary image.
10. **Voice and signifier:** speech is not just semantic content. The graph retains the material and enunciative dimensions through which the Other's address affects the subject.

### Developmental note

[DEVELOPMENTAL NOTE: Appendix A reproduces the later complete graph for orientation. When using this corpus to answer chronological questions, the reconstruction of individual Seminar V chapters should take priority over the complete graph. The later notation should not be projected backward as though already stabilized at the opening of the 1957-1958 seminar.]

### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, Book V: Formations of the Unconscious*, Appendix A, printed p. 485.
- Jacques-Alain Miller, editor's note in the same volume, on the subsequent definitive formulation of the graph in "Subversion of the Subject".

## Appendix B. Explanation of the Schemas

**Primary source:** Polity 2017, printed pp. 486-490  
**Meeting date:** 31 January 1958  
**Status:** Expanded editorial reproduction of Paul Lemoine's notes from a small-group discussion; not a regular seminar lesson and not a written text by Lacan

### Source status

This appendix requires a stronger provenance warning than an ordinary seminar chapter. According to the source, on 31 January 1958, between weeks eleven and twelve, Lacan met with a small group who had asked for further explanation of the schemas. The discussion was not taken down in full. Paul Lemoine's notes, consisting of a summary and drawings, are the only record and are reproduced in expanded form. The source explicitly warns that this is neither one of Lacan's written texts nor a class from the Seminar.

The appendix is nonetheless valuable because it states compactly several structural principles that the seminar develops at greater length.

### 1. The signifying chain

The analytic field cannot be defined without the structuring function of the signifier. The speaking subject is constituted in relation to the signifying chain and cannot be separated from discourse. The human subject is therefore distinguished from animal life not by a larger repertoire of signals but by insertion into a chain in which one signifier refers to another and in which signification is produced through their relations.

The appendix links this directly to the Other. Subjects are caught in the Other, identified here with the field of the unconscious, and access to the unconscious occurs through the Other's intervention. The point anticipates the later formula that the unconscious is the discourse of the Other: the subject's most intimate determinations are articulated in a field that is not identical with conscious self-possession.

The Name-of-the-Father is presented as a decisive signifying knot. The paternal function is not derived from the biological father as an empirical person. A signification emerging from the signifying chain converges on this signifier. Only through this symbolic function can the father enter specifically human intersubjectivity.

This has direct technical implications. The notes criticize analytic approaches that privilege the imaginary relationship between analyst and analysand, including Bouvet's emphasis on the homosexual aspect of transference and imaginary fellatio. The problem is not that imaginary relations are unreal. It is that analysis goes astray if it treats the ego-to-ego relation as the whole field. Schema L and the developing graph are designed precisely to ask what traverses this imaginary axis from the Other toward the subject.

### 2. This year's schema

The appendix then reduces the year's construction to the elementary signifying chain. A horizontal line of signifiers is placed over a line of signifieds:

```text
S  ....................
-----------------------
s  ....................
```

The point is not that signifier and signified proceed in parallel synchrony. The line must be **bent** to represent retroaction.

[FIGURE: Bent signifying chain]

Source location: Appendix B, printed p. 487.

Description: a curved arrow bends back over the linear chain. The curve indicates that later signifiers retroact on earlier signified effects. Meaning is not fixed at the instant each word is uttered.

The next figure marks two points, conventionally represented as `p` and `p'`. When the sentence reaches the later point `p`, a result is obtained retroactively at the earlier point `p'`. Lacan's example is the line from Racine's *Athaliah*: the sentence's final words determine the sense of what preceded them. This is the same logic that underpins the quilting point and the analysis of the witticism earlier in Seminar V.

[FIGURE: Retroaction between `p` and `p'`]

Source location: Appendix B, printed p. 488.

Description: an upper arc moves forward toward `p` while a smaller return arc loops back toward `p'`. The figure makes visible the claim that signification is constituted retroactively at punctuation or completion.

A further line is then introduced to represent **the intention of discourse**. Speech is not detached from the concrete subject who utters it. The signifying chain therefore has to be crossed by another trajectory expressing the subject's movement into discourse.

[FIGURE: Intention of discourse crossing the signifying chain]

Source location: Appendix B, printed p. 488.

Description: a vertically rising and returning curve intersects the bent signifying line. The shape anticipates the elementary cell from which the fuller graph will be built.

The term that allows discourse to be inserted into the human subject is **desire**. Desire begins at the same level as the movement that sets the signifying chain in operation. It is not an object added after language. The rest of the schema is organized from the conjunction of signifying articulation and desire.

The appendix situates the infant's first cry inside this structure. The child connects with the mother, from whom the use of the signifying chain will be acquired. The encounter with the Other is projected onto the elementary crossing and produces the message. The action of speaking then has retroactive effects on the subject's desire.

[FIGURE: Early complete elementary schema with message `M` and Other `A`]

Source location: Appendix B, printed p. 489.

Description: the curved signifying path intersects a second trajectory. The upper circular points are labelled `M` and `A`; below them are `β'` and `β`, connected by a horizontal arrow. The lower short-circuit `A-β-β'-M` designates the level at which the subject can be treated as an animal, while the fuller crossing introduces the specifically human field of signification and desire. The specular relation `a-a'` is located on this lower, imaginary level.

The distinction is important. Human subjectivity does not abolish animal functions. It overlays and reorganizes them through the signifier. The imaginary confrontation remains, but it is crossed by the symbolic structure.

### 3. Concerning the Oedipus complex

The final part of the appendix uses the schema to situate the imaginary mother-phallus-child triad developed in Seminar IV. Lacan insists that pre-Oedipal relations can be described only from the standpoint of a subject who is already structurally situated by Oedipus. The schema is therefore not a developmental chronology in which the imaginary simply comes first and the symbolic later. It is a structural map that allows earlier relations to be located retrospectively.

Masculine homosexuality is used as an example. The relation to the mother is not adequately explained by the formula of a "phallic woman". The decisive issue is the mother's relation to the father's speech and therefore to the symbolic function that mediates desire. The schema allows this relation to be plotted among `S`, `a`, `a'`, and `A` rather than reduced to a bodily characteristic of the mother.

The same framework clarifies identification with the father at the end of Oedipus. Identification is not mere imitation of the empirical father. It arises from the way symbolic and imaginary triangles are superimposed. The subject's paradoxical relations to the penis, including its requirement in the eroticized object or its fantasmatic threat, can be located within the combined structure.

[FIGURE: Superposition of the symbolic and imaginary triangles]

Source location: Appendix B, printed p. 490.

Description: two vertically stacked curved cells are crossed by diagonal and vertical lines, with arrowheads indicating the directions of the circuits. The figure superimposes the schema in which the code turns back upon the message with the earlier quadrilateral/triangular relations. Its function is to show how identification emerges from the conjunction of the imaginary relation and the symbolic relation to the Other.

The appendix concludes with the striking image that identification is like Dante's condemned lovers who kiss and each becomes the other. The metaphor emphasizes that identification is a transformation in position within a relation, not the simple acquisition of a trait from an isolated object.

### Relation to the seminar as a whole

Appendix B is especially useful for understanding the continuity between the first part of Seminar V and the later graph of desire. The early discussions of sentence, code, message, wit, quilting, and retroaction are not abandoned when Lacan turns to Oedipus, phallus, and neurosis. They provide the elementary geometry from which the later graph is constructed. Desire is progressively inserted into that geometry, and the imaginary relation is preserved but subordinated to a wider symbolic structure.

Because the appendix comes from summary notes rather than a full transcript, it should be used to clarify the architecture of the schemas, not as the sole textual basis for fine-grained claims about Lacan's wording on 31 January 1958.

### Sources used

- Jacques Lacan, *The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, Book V: Formations of the Unconscious*, Appendix B, printed pp. 486-490.
- Editorial provenance statement introducing Appendix B.

## Editorial orientation relevant to the seminar's structure

Jacques-Alain Miller's editor's note supplies several chronological anchors useful for interpreting the completed reconstruction without turning it into a cross-source synthesis.

- The graph developed during Seminar V later acquired its definitive form in "Subversion of the Subject and the Dialectic of Desire", written in 1962.
- The first part of Seminar V is closely connected with Lacan's 1957 "The Instance of the Letter in the Unconscious, or Reason Since Freud".
- After the first seven lessons, Lacan wrote "On a Question Prior to Any Possible Treatment of Psychosis", which helps explain the prominence of foreclosure and the paternal metaphor in the January sessions.
- During the February break he wrote "The Youth of Gide", echoed when the seminar resumes with Part III.
- The Part III lessons and the session of 7 May are connected to the Munich lecture "The Signification of the Phallus" of 9 May 1958.
- The final clinical part coincides with the preparation of "The Direction of the Treatment and the Principles of Its Power", presented at Royaumont in July 1958.

These points are used only as editorial chronology. They do not replace the Seminar V text, and later written formulations should not be silently substituted for the formulations reconstructed session by session above.


## Internal cross-reference index

- **Wit / Witz / witticism / joke:** Chapters I-VII. The opening sequence develops the signifier through Freud's joke mechanisms, portmanteau formations, recognition by the Other, production of sense, and the distinction between empty and signifying speech.
- **Famillionaire and related verbal formations:** Chapters I-III, with further implications for metaphor, metonymy, message, and code across Chapters IV-VII.
- **Signifier and signified:** Chapters I-VII; XII-XIII; XVII-XIX; Appendices A-B. Especially important in Chapters I-II, XII, XIX, and Appendix B.
- **Signifying chain:** Chapters I-VII; XII-XIII; XIX; XXII; XXVI; Appendices A-B.
- **Metaphor:** Chapters I-II, VIII-IX, XI-XII, XVII-XIX. The paternal metaphor is treated most directly in Chapters VIII-IX.
- **Metonymy:** Chapters I-VII, XI-XIII, XVII-XIX, XX-XXII. Includes the metonymic status of desire and the phallus in the 1957-1958 formulation.
- **Message and code:** Chapters I-VII, VIII, XI, XIX, XXII; Appendix B. These terms provide a bridge from the theory of wit to the paternal function and later to the graph of desire.
- **Point de capiton / quilting / retroaction:** Chapters I-VII and Appendix B, with consequences for the later graph construction.
- **The Other:** Chapters I-VII; VIII-XI; XIX-XXVIII; Appendices A-B. The Other is successively treated as locus of the code, locus of recognition, locus of law, and locus in relation to which desire is articulated.
- **Foreclosure:** Chapter VIII, with supporting consequences in Chapters IX-XI.
- **Name-of-the-Father:** Chapters VIII-IX, XI, XXVII; Appendix B.
- **Paternal metaphor:** Chapters VIII-IX, with further Oedipal elaboration in Chapters X-XI and schematic restatement in Chapter XXVII and Appendix B.
- **Oedipus complex / three moments of Oedipus:** Chapters IX-XI; later consequences in Chapters XV-XVIII, XXV, XXVII-XXVIII, and Appendix B.
- **Castration:** Chapters VIII-XIII; XIV-XIX; XXV; XXVII-XXVIII.
- **Frustration / privation / castration distinction:** Chapters VIII-XII, especially where Seminar IV's object-lack distinctions are reorganized through the paternal metaphor.
- **Phallus:** Chapters VIII-XIX; XXII-XXVIII; Appendices A-B. Key concentrations occur in Chapters XI, XIV-XIX, XXV, and XXVII.
- **Imaginary phallus and symbolic function of the phallus:** Chapters VIII-XI, XIV-XIX, XXV, XXVII.
- **Mother / child / father triad:** Chapters VIII-XI; XV; Appendix B.
- **Need, demand, and desire:** Chapters XIV-XIX and especially Chapters XX-XXVIII; consolidated in Appendices A-B.
- **Demand for love:** Chapters XX-XXV, especially the clinical discussions of hysteria, obsession, transference, and suggestion.
- **Desire:** Throughout the seminar; major concentrations in Chapters XIV, XVII-XIX, XX-XXVIII, and Appendices A-B.
- **Desire of the Other:** Chapters VI-VII, XI, XIX, XX-XXIV, XXVI-XXVIII; Appendix A.
- **Graph of desire:** Early cells and precursors in Chapters I, VI-VII; major development in Chapters XIX-XXIV and XXVI; consolidated in Appendix A and explained structurally in Appendix B.
- **Fantasy:** Chapters XIII, XVII-XIX, XXII-XXIII, XXVI-XXVIII. Chapter XIII provides the major transition from image/signifier to fantasy.
- **Symptom:** Chapters XVIII, XX-XXI, XXVII-XXVIII. Chapter XXVII is the principal treatment of exiting via the symptom.
- **Hysteria:** Chapters XX-XXII, XXIV-XXV, with the butcher's beautiful wife as the central dream example in Chapter XX.
- **Obsession / obsessional desire:** Chapters XXIII-XXVIII, with clinical and transference consequences extending across the final part.
- **The butcher's beautiful wife:** Chapter XX.
- **"Still waters run deep" dreams:** Chapter XXI.
- **Major Freud joke examples:** Chapters I-VII.
- **Major dream analyses:** Chapters XX-XXI, with other dream and fantasy material appearing earlier where relevant.
- **Transference:** Chapters XXIV-XXV and Appendix B.
- **Suggestion:** Chapter XXIV.
- **Identification:** Chapters X-XI, XV-XVIII, XXIII, XXVIII; Appendix B.
- **Ideal ego and ego ideal:** Chapter XVI, with supporting identification material in Chapters XV-XVIII.
- **Insignias of the ideal:** Chapter XVI.
- **Jouissance:** Chapters XIV-XIX and the final clinical sequence where the relation among desire, demand, and phallic function is developed. Interpret these uses within the 1957-1958 conceptual horizon rather than through later Lacanian doctrine.
- **Sexual difference in Seminar V's period-specific formulation:** Chapters XI, XV-XVII, XXV, and Appendix B. These discussions are historical formulations and should not be replaced by Lacan's later formulas of sexuation.
- **Male homosexuality in Lacan's 1958 Oedipal theorization:** Chapter XI and Appendix B. The reconstruction marks the historical and clinical limits of these claims.
- **Circuits of desire:** Chapter XXVI.
- **Exit via the symptom:** Chapter XXVII.
- **"You are the one you hate" / title homophony:** Chapter XXVIII.
- **Schemas and diagrams:** Chapters I, II, VI-VIII, IX-XIII, XVII, XIX, XX-XXIV, XXVI-XXVIII, and especially Appendices A-B. Where the source's visual structure mattered, the relevant rendered page was checked and a descriptive reconstruction supplied.

## Key terms appearing in this file

`A` / big Other; `a` / little other where used in the Seminar V schemas; barred subject; castration; code; condensation; demand; desire; desire of the Other; displacement; ego ideal; fantasy; foreclosure; formations of the unconscious; frustration; graph of desire; hysteria; identification; ideal ego; imaginary; jouissance; law; message; metaphor; metonymy; mother; Name-of-the-Father; need; neurosis; obsession; Oedipus complex; Other; paternal metaphor; phallus; point de capiton; privation; retroaction; signification; signified; signifier; signifying chain; suggestion; symptom; transference; wit; *Witz*; *trait d'esprit*; *mot d'esprit*; *Verwerfung* where relevant to foreclosure; symbolic; real; imaginary; *Une Femme de Non-Recevoir*; *famillionaire*; *Miglionaire*.

## Provenance / source note

The controlling source for this reconstruction is Jacques Lacan, *Formations of the Unconscious: The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, Book V*, edited by Jacques-Alain Miller, translated by Russell Grigg, Polity Press, 2017. The published English edition controls chapter order, chapter titles, pagination, terminology, editorial organization, appendices, and the wording used for source references.

Cormac Gallagher's English translation from unedited French typescripts was used only as an alternate source. It was consulted for session-date confirmation in Chapters I-XIII and, in Chapter XI, to document the discrepancy between the Polity date and Gallagher's date. Gallagher was not used as a parallel base text for Chapters XIV-XXVIII or the appendices.

The reconstruction also uses editorial material internal to the Polity volume where it clarifies source status, chronology, diagrams, or title wordplay. This includes Jacques-Alain Miller's editorial note concerning the later definitive form of the graph, Russell Grigg's translator note on the Chapter XXVIII title, and the provenance statement attached to Appendix B. No outside secondary literature was used to construct the chapter reconstructions.

## Processing notes and uncertainties

This file was produced as a Mode B exhaustive structured reconstruction, not as a verbatim transcription. Paraphrase is the default, while short exact phrases, puns, formulas, title wordplay, and technical notation are retained only where wording is conceptually important.

The source was processed without global Optical Character Recognition (OCR). Parsed text was used as the normal basis. Rendered page images were inspected locally where diagrams, formulas, graph structure, or visual notation required confirmation. No unresolved figure or formula issue remains in the completed file.

One material source uncertainty remains: the date attached to Chapter XI. The Polity edition prints `20 January 1958`, while the Gallagher transcript gives Wednesday 29 January 1958, which fits the weekly sequence between 22 January and 5 February. The chapter records 29 January as the session date while preserving the discrepancy explicitly in an editorial note. This has no effect on the reconstructed conceptual content.

Appendix B carries a separate provenance qualification rather than a content uncertainty. Its "Explanation of the Schemas" is based on Paul Lemoine's summary notes and drawings from the small-group discussion of 31 January 1958, not on a full transcript and not on a regular seminar lesson. It is therefore used to clarify the architecture of the schemas, not as sole evidence for fine-grained claims about Lacan's exact wording.

Later Lacanian terminology has not been used to overwrite the 1957-1958 formulations. Where later developments are mentioned, they are explicitly marked as developmental or editorial orientation rather than attributed retrospectively to Seminar V.
